pages.observedMeaningfulContent: Title: Lecture 21, Linear Control of Manipulators, with author and institution.
Learning objective is understanding the basics of linear control.
Contents list feedback, second-order systems, control-law partitioning, trajectory following and disturbances.
Linear differential-equation models support linear control methods. Actual manipulator dynamics are nonlinear; justified approximations can permit linear theory.

Open-loop diagram: trajectory generator supplies desired position, velocity and acceleration to model-based torque computation. Torque is M(Θ_d)Θ̈_d+V(Θ_d,Θ̇_d)+G(Θ_d). No measured-output feedback branch exists. Perfect-model idealization also needs compatible initial state and no unmodeled disturbance. Stepper motors are an example of open-loop use, not universally incapable of feedback.

Feedback diagram returns actual Θ and Θ̇ to the controller; trajectory generator supplies three desired signals, torque drives robot. Signals are N×1 vectors, N is joint count. Sensors measure joint position and sometimes velocity. The repeated desired-only inverse-dynamics formula is a feedforward component, not a complete feedback law.

Servo error is E=Θ_d−Θ and Ė=Θ̇_d−Θ̇. A 4× PDF detail confirms the desired-velocity dot is present; OCR can miss it. Stability is explained informally as keeping errors small under moderate disturbances. Feedback must be designed for stability; its mere presence is not a guarantee.
Manipulator control is coupled MIMO. Independent joint control replaces it approximately with N SISO loops. The arm photograph is illustrative and adds no numbered kinematic data.

Mass–spring–damper diagram has positive x to the right and restoring/viscous forces −kx and −bẋ. The homogeneous equation is mẍ+bẋ+kx=0. m is mass, b viscous damping coefficient, k stiffness. Weak spring/heavy damping can be sluggish; stiff spring/light damping can oscillate, with formal threshold on following slides.
Characteristic polynomial ms²+bs+k=0 and roots [−b±√(b²−4mk)]/(2m). Pole locations determine response. Stability classifications require the relevant physical/gain signs, not discriminant alone.

Positive-parameter damping classification: discriminant positive gives real unequal overdamped poles; negative gives complex underdamped poles; zero gives critical damping. Fastest non-oscillatory language requires a fixed natural-frequency/model comparison, not arbitrary initial conditions or arbitrary design limits. The interactive link targets a local second_order_simulator_v2.html file not present in supplied files; no executable code is printed on this page.

Distinct real-root solution is c₁e^(s₁t)+c₂e^(s₂t), constants from initial position and velocity. Plot shows two negative real poles, s₁ farther left than s₂. The farther-left term decays faster for stable real poles; slow-pole dominance needs a nonzero slow-mode coefficient and a sufficiently late time.

Conjugate roots λ±iμ are expanded using Euler’s identity into e^(λt)[C₁cos(μt)+C₂sin(μt)]. Real motion requires the appropriate conjugate coefficients; C₁=c₁+c₂ and C₂=i(c₁−c₂). The final real constants can be written r cosδ and r sinδ.

Amplitude-phase form is r e^(λt) cos(μt−δ), with r from the real cosine/sine coefficients and δ=atan2(sine coefficient,cosine coefficient). The slide reuses lowercase constants after uppercase constants on page 649; do not apply that real amplitude formula directly to the earlier complex coefficients. Pole diagram shows a left-half-plane conjugate pair and decaying oscillations; decay assumes λ<0.

Normalized polynomial s²+2ζω_n s+ω_n²=0. ζ=b/(2√km), ω_n=√(k/m), λ=−ζω_n, and μ=ω_n√(1−ζ²) for the underdamped case. No damping has b=ζ=0; positive critical damping has ζ=1. Natural frequency is not damped oscillation frequency.

Repeated-root solution is (c₁+c₂t)e^(−bt/(2m)); the independent t factor is essential. Plot shows coincident negative real poles and non-oscillatory decay. The polynomial-times-exponential limit uses a>0. Fastest-response wording has the same scope qualification as page 647.
A right-directed actuator force f is added to the mass–spring–damper diagram, giving mẍ+bẋ+kx=f. Sensing and actuation can change the natural response.

Direct zero-reference feedback is f=−k_p x−k_v ẋ. The diagram routes position through k_p and velocity through k_v to negative summing inputs. Effective coefficients become b′=b+k_v and k′=k+k_p; inertia remains m.

Critical direct-feedback design uses b′=2√(mk′). Gains themselves may be negative while total effective damping/stiffness stay positive. Example m=b=k=1, desired k′=16 gives k_p=15,k_v=7 and repeated poles −4. For m>0, asymptotic stability requires both b′>0 and k′>0; equality cases need separate treatment.
Control-law partitioning separates a model-based portion that simplifies the plant from a servo portion designed around the simplified model.

Partitioned force f=αf′+β uses α=m and β=bẋ+kx. Exact matching cancels damping/stiffness, yielding ẍ=f′, a normalized acceleration input. Physical parameters remain in the model-based part. The actual plant is not physically stripped of mass, damping or stiffness.

Servo f′=−k_v ẋ−k_p x yields ẍ+k_v ẋ+k_p x=0. Critical damping is k_v=2√k_p for k_p>0. These normalized gains have different units and values from direct force-feedback gains; parameter independence assumes exact model compensation.

Partitioned diagram shows servo negative feedback, multiplication by m, and positive cancellation feedforward bẋ+kx. Example m=b=k=1,k_p=16 gives α=1,β=ẋ+x,k_v=8. Combined physical force equals −15x−7ẋ, matching the earlier direct design.

Trajectory following needs smooth desired x_d, ẋ_d and ẍ_d. Error e=x_d−x; servo acceleration f′=ẍ_d+k_v ė+k_p e. The feedback acts in error coordinates and includes desired acceleration feedforward.

Substitution yields ë+k_v ė+k_p e=0 under exact unit-mass model. Diagram has desired-minus-actual comparators, positive error gains and acceleration feedforward, then model-based scaling/cancellation. Any response wording means choosing this ideal second-order polynomial, not arbitrary realizable hardware performance.

Forced error model is printed ë+k_v ė+k_p e=f_dist. A high-resolution detail confirms the physical disturbance arrow enters a MINUS summing input after the mass gain. Thus a resisting physical force F_dist gives normalized error forcing F_dist/m; the reused symbol needs an explicit mass/unit convention. This is a forced second-order error model.

BIBO means bounded disturbance magnitude implies bounded error for a stable closed-loop transfer function. Printed max f_dist<a omits absolute value; an upper bound alone does not bound negative excursions. Closed-loop stability must be assumed, and bounded does not mean zero error.

For constant normalized error forcing d and stable positive k_p,k_v, steady-state derivatives vanish and e_ss=d/k_p. Larger positive k_p reduces magnitude for a fixed nonzero d. Error is never zero requires nonzero disturbance and finite gain; it is not true for zero forcing.

Integral action adds k_i∫e dt to servo and error equation. High-resolution rendering confirms the differentiated equation has e triple-dot and f_dist DOT on the right. Constant forcing has zero derivative after its onset. Stable steady state with k_i≠0 can yield e=0. The characteristic polynomial is s³+k_v s²+k_p s+k_i; positive gains alone do not guarantee stability. Initial integrator state and onset discontinuities must not be erased by differentiation.

Summary repeats linear approximation, feedback/MIMO-to-SISO approximation, damping classes, partitioning, trajectory errors and disturbance/integral control. Link it to the substantive earlier questions rather than padding with duplicate recall.
